_about: Synthetic sample lesson written for LessonTrace. Not a recording of a real class. Times are generated from word counts by scripts/seed_demo.py; the findings below were written by hand and pass through the same evidence validator as model output.
title: Calculus I — An Introduction to Limits (sample)
slides:
An Introduction to Limits
Calculus I, Week 3
Today: the idea of a limit; a famous example, sine x over x; one-sided limits; when a limit does not exist

The idea of a limit
A limit describes the value a function approaches as the input approaches a point
The function does not need to be defined at that point
Notation: lim f(x) = L as x approaches a
Everyday picture: walking toward a door without stepping through it

A famous example: sine x over x
f(x) = sin(x) / x is not defined at x = 0
Table of values: x = 0.5, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001
The ratio gets closer and closer to 1
Graph: a hole at the point (0, 1)
Squeeze theorem (proof next week)

One-sided limits
Left-hand limit: x approaches a from below
Right-hand limit: x approaches a from above
The two-sided limit exists only if both sides agree
Example: the step function at zero
Infinite limits and vertical asymptotes

Summary and practice
A limit is about approaching, not arriving
Check both sides before you claim a limit exists
Practice: problems 1 to 6 on the worksheet
Next time: limit laws
script: Good morning everyone, let's get started.
Last week we finished our review of functions, and today we begin the first really new idea of this course, which is the limit.
Here is the plan for today.
First I want to give you the idea of a limit in plain words.
Then we will look at a famous example, sine x over x.
After that we will talk about one-sided limits, and finally about when a limit does not exist.
By the end of the hour you should be able to read a limit statement and say in your own words what it means.
A limit describes the value a function approaches as the input approaches some point.
Notice that I said approaches, not equals.
The function does not even need to be defined at that point.
Think about walking toward a door.
With every step you cover half of the remaining distance.
You get closer and closer to the door, but you never actually step through it.
The door is the limit of your position.
We write it like this: the limit of f of x, as x approaches a, equals L.
Read it out loud with me: the limit of f of x, as x approaches a, equals L.
The letter a is where the input is heading, and the letter L is where the output is heading.
Does that make sense to everyone?
Take the function f of x equals sine x divided by x.
What happens if we plug in zero?
We get zero over zero, which is not defined, so the function has no value at zero.
But we can still ask what the function is approaching.
Look at the table on this slide.
When x is zero point five, the ratio is about zero point nine five nine.
When x is zero point one, it is about zero point nine nine eight.
When x is zero point zero one, it is zero point nine nine nine nine eight.
The ratio gets closer and closer to one.
So what does this limit equal?
On the graph you can see a smooth curve with a tiny hole at the point zero comma one.
The hole is exactly the door from our picture: the curve walks up to it from both sides and never steps through.
We will prove this properly next week, so for today just trust the table.
Before we move on, I want you to try one yourselves.
Take thirty seconds and work out, with your neighbour, what x squared minus one over x minus one approaches as x goes to one.
We factored the top, so it cancels and you get x plus one, and that goes to two.
Exactly, the factor x minus one cancels, and what is left is x plus one, which approaches two.
And did anyone try a table instead?
We did, we tried zero point nine and one point one and got one point nine and two point one.
Good, so two different methods agree, and that should make you more confident in the answer.
Notice again that the function is not defined at one, and the limit does not care.
Now let us move on to one-sided limits.
Sometimes it matters which direction you come from.
The left-hand limit means x approaches a from below, through smaller values.
The right-hand limit means x approaches a from above, through larger values.
The two-sided limit exists only if both sides agree.
Is the left limit always the same as the right limit?
Good question, and the answer is no.
Think of the step function, which is zero for negative inputs and one for positive inputs.
From the left you are walking along the floor at height zero.
From the right you are walking along a shelf at height one.
So the left-hand limit is zero and the right-hand limit is one.
They disagree, so we say the two-sided limit at zero does not exist.
Why do we care about this?
Because later, when we define continuity and the derivative, both of them are built out of limits that must agree from both sides.
Let me summarise what we did today.
A limit is about approaching, not arriving.
The function does not need to be defined at the point.
And before you claim that a limit exists, check both sides.
For practice, please do problems one to six on the worksheet before Thursday.
Problems five and six are one-sided limits, so look back at the step function if you get stuck.
Next time we will learn the limit laws, which let us compute limits without building a table every time.
Thank you, see you on Thursday.
titles: Opening and plan for the lesson
The idea of a limit: approaching, not equalling
Sine x over x near zero
Pair task: a limit by factoring and by table
The step function: when the two sides disagree

findings.observation: The lesson opens with a spoken outline of its four parts and states what students should be able to do by the end.
findings.suggestion: Keep this opening. Returning to the same outline at each transition would let students see where they are in the plan.
quotes: Here is the plan for today.
By the end of the hour you should be able to read a limit statement and say in your own words what it means.

findings.observation: The closing summary restates the two main ideas in short sentences and links the homework problems to the step function example from the lesson.
findings.suggestion: Consider asking a student to state one of the summary points first, then confirming it, so the recap also works as a quick check.
quotes: A limit is about approaching, not arriving.
Problems five and six are one-sided limits, so look back at the step function if you get stuck.

findings.observation: The question about the value of the limit was answered by the teacher about half a second after it was asked, before any student responded.
findings.suggestion: Pause for a few seconds after asking, or ask students to write their answer down before you confirm it.
quotes: So what does this limit equal?

findings.observation: The two comprehension checks were whole-class yes/no questions, and the lesson continued within about a second each time without a student reply.
findings.suggestion: Replace one of them with a question that needs a content answer, for example asking a student to say what the letters a and L stand for.
quotes: Does that make sense to everyone?

findings.observation: In the pair task, students had time to work before the question was asked, two different student methods were heard, and the second was invited explicitly.
findings.suggestion: This pattern produced the longest student contributions of the lesson; a similar short task could be used in the sine x over x part.
quotes: And did anyone try a table instead?
Good, so two different methods agree, and that should make you more confident in the answer.

findings.observation: The door picture introduced with the definition is picked up again when the graph of sine x over x is described, tying the new example back to the first idea.
findings.suggestion: The same picture could be reused once more for the step function, where the two sides walk toward different doors.
quotes: You get closer and closer to the door, but you never actually step through it.
The hole is exactly the door from our picture: the curve walks up to it from both sides and never steps through.

findings.observation: A student's question about whether the two one-sided limits always agree is answered directly and then illustrated with a concrete floor-and-shelf description of the step function.
findings.suggestion: After the illustration, asking the student who raised the question to restate the conclusion would show whether the explanation landed.
quotes: Good question, and the answer is no.
From the right you are walking along a shelf at height one.

findings.observation: The slide for the sine x over x example lists the squeeze theorem; in the lesson it is referred to only as a proof that will come next week, without being named.
findings.suggestion: Either name the theorem when deferring it, so students can connect the slide to what was said, or remove the line from this week's slide.
quotes: We will prove this properly next week, so for today just trust the table.

findings.observation: The one-sided limits slide ends with a line on infinite limits and vertical asymptotes, which is not mentioned while that slide is being discussed.
findings.suggestion: Tell students whether that line is for a later lesson, or move it to the slide deck for the session where it is taught.
quotes: They disagree, so we say the two-sided limit at zero does not exist.
